Now we need to invert the distribution. We observed n = Σnᵢ total successes, each trial has success rate p = Σ2⁻ᵏⁱ.

Bayesian approach: With a flat prior on X, the posterior is:

X∣n  ∼  Gamma(n+1,p)X∣n∼Gamma(n+1,p)

where p is the rate parameter. The 95% credible interval is:

X∈[χ2(n+1),0.02522p,  χ2(n+1),0.97522p]X∈[2pχ2(n+1),0.0252​​,2pχ2(n+1),0.9752​​]

Gaussian approximation (for n ≳ 10):

X∈np⋅(1±1.96n)X∈pn​⋅(1±n​1.96​)

or equivalently:

X∈[n−1.96np,  n+1.96np]X∈[pn−1.96n​​,pn+1.96n​​]

Example: You observe n₁ = 8 at 2⁻¹⁰ and n₂ = 3 at 2⁻⁸.

  • n = 11, p = 1/1024 + 1/256 = 5/1024
  • Point estimate: X̂ = 11 · 1024/5 ≈ 2253
  • 95% CI: 2253 · (1 ± 1.96/√11) ≈ [920, 3586]

Intuition: The width scales as 1/√n — more observed successes means tighter bounds. The relative uncertainty is roughly ±2/√n, so you need ~400 total successes to pin down the trial count to ±10%.
